tweets.text:
Our recent piece on investing strategies has a lot of folks saying that passive investing is the same thing as dollar cost averaging. 

Passive investing is when a fund offers the performance of a benchmark. Active investing is when a fund tries to beat the performance of a benchmark. 

Dollar cost averaging (DCA) is simple setting fixed dates to invest in a passive fund, or an active fund, or a stock, or even many stocks.

DCA helps reduce market timing risk and is generally how most investors go about investing anyway as they receive income from employment.

If you have a lump sum of money, research shows that's it's a marginally better idea to invest it rather than wait, though we suggest you might take a hybrid approach which is psychologically more appealing for investors.

tweets.text:
If an account on X does nothing but post about a single ticker, that's a big red flag.

Why?

Well for one, there is nothing stopping an investor relations firm from creating numerous accounts that engage in this behavior and trying to create "awareness" around a stock.

You might argue this isn't problematic, but this creates hype, not intrinsic value. It creates noise. It creates volatility.

$ZETA is one of the most hyped stocks on X right now. When we called attention to this fact recently, some folks come around and started to get really irate.

Why is that?

If an account on X spends all their time pumping a single stock, they might be doing that because they're passionate about the company. Or they're chasing clout. Or maybe even they're getting some kickbacks from the company. You'll probably never know, because they're not obligated to tell you. Nobody is checking. So when numerous accounts do this, you have to wonder.

Another good example would be $ASTS. Is this a cult stock, a stock community, a concerted effort to pump the stock by an "investor relations consultancy," or a combination of all three? Post something negative about the company and you you'll quickly see that whatever it is, it's definitely not a community that promotes critical thinking.

The point is simply this.

People who constantly pump the same stock cannot be counted on to be objective in their analysis. They lose credibility by doing this. Their words carry less weight.

Always be most critical of the stocks you're most bullish about.

Class action lawsuits are often leveled too liberally upon firms but they merit some scrutiny nonetheless. 

The accusations are that Keel Infrastructure $KEEL (formerly known as Bitfarms) current and former executives misled investors about the company’s finances.

Specifically, they say the company:

---) Had weak internal accounting controls.
---) Wrongly counted money from selling Bitcoin as “operating cash flow” (which makes the business look healthier) instead of “investing cash flow.”
---) Overstated how well and how quickly it was fixing these accounting problems (especially one involving warrants issued in 2021).

When the truth came out in late 2024 (the company announced it had to restate several years of financial statements), the stock price dropped and investors lost money. 

The lawsuit also claims management sold some of their own shares while allegedly knowing the problems were bigger than disclosed.

So whether this costs $KEEL money isn't the issue here. It's about integrity. If a company management team behaves this way once, they'll likely do it again. Even if a company removes their management team, the apple doesn't fall far from the tree and bad habits often persist.

We wouldn't even consider investing in $KEEL until this gets resolved in their favor.

tweets.text:
Posts we've made lately that applied some critical thinking to names like $SOFI solicited a lot of attacks.

Why?

Here's how this works.

It all starts with accounts that establish themselves as "authorities" simply by posting constantly using the company cashtags. You see this a lot with $ZETA lately. They'll make it very clear that they think they're the leader of the pack. Once they have enough momentum they may even get the CEO on for an interview which they then point to as proof of their legitimacy. 

These "thought leaders" attract large audiences of retail investors who start to follow the stock more closely. These folks will start parroting the same talking points. Many will start to overweight the stock instead of taking a responsible approach to investing. 

For smaller stocks, this may lead to shorter term share price appreciation though intrinsic value hasn't changed.

What then happens is a natural product of psychology. These retail investors have pinned so much of their "wealth" on the stock (these are usually small accounts) that anyone being the slightest bit critical of their sacred cow is seen as a threat to their future imagined wealth.

Now imagine someone managing a portfolio of stocks and one of the names is $ZETA or $SOFI. They're much more likely to perceive criticisms as a good thing. In fact, being critical of the stocks you're most bullish about is the sign of a mature investor.

These large "though leaders" who focus on single stocks cannot be objective by definition. This means those who follow them start to lose their ability to think critically about investments. Worse, they start to establish bad investing practices.

If you post something critical about a stock and get attacked for it, now you know why. You're seen as a threat to someone's bad investing practices.

The strong revenue growth over at Symbotic $SYM is nullified by their heavy dependence on Walmart $WMT while the other two names we’ve been watching over the years – AutoStore $AUTO and Ocado $OCDO – are not making hay while the sun shines. 

The Chinese are though, and Geek+ $2590 looks like an interesting way to play the growth of warehouse automation across multiple geographies. 

We’ll be scrutinizing their next earnings release a lot closer given there’s a fair amount to like about this company.
